sheep_herdwick.text: How did YOU get up here? I came for the grass. The cairn is an accident.

ld_shepherd.text: The Herdwicks 'heft' to the hill: each ewe knows her own bit of fell without a fence, and she passes it to her lambs. If a flock's lost, you can't just replace it. You have to wait three generations.
My dog's name is Fly. She knows more about the sheep than I do, and she's polite about it.

ld_walker.text: Eight hundred metres up and the weather's changed four times. Waterproofs on, waterproofs off, and now a hat with a bobble. The Lakes make you a layer person.
There's a rule: Wainwright's guides list 214 fells. People try to climb them all. They're called Wainwright-baggers. It's a hobby and also a punishment.

ld_slater.text: Green slate: the colour of rain on a good day. We split it by hand, one layer at a time. You can tell the good bit by the ring when you tap it.
Roofs in the Lakes last a century. Roofing slate's the only thing here that doesn't mind the wet.

ld_poet.text: I wandered lonely as a cloud, but the cloud was quite crowded. Mind you, daffodils do take the day off from the weather.
A famous poet lived near here and walked about 175,000 miles in his life. He wrote his verses in his head as he went. He never once brought a map.

ld_ranger.text: I'm told off for walking off the path, and then I tell off the walkers for walking off the path. It's a very circular job.
Look at the pass in front of you. See the cairn of stones? Please leave them stacked. If you must add one, add a little one.
